questions.question: Which of the following is not a solid solution?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Aerated drinks

A **solid solution** is a homogeneous mixture in which the solvent is a solid: brass (Cu–Zn) and bronze (Cu–Sn) are substitutional solid solutions, and a hydrated salt such as $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ is a solid in which water molecules occupy definite sites in the crystal — a solid solution of water in the salt. **Aerated drinks** are a gas dissolved in a **liquid**, so they are a liquid solution, not a solid one.

questions.question: What is the molality of a solution formed when 58.5 g of NaCl is dissolved in 200 g of water?
questions.answer:
**(C)** 0.005 M *(see note — the question is defective)*

Moles of NaCl, with $M=23+35.5=58.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$:

$$n=\frac{58.5}{58.5}=1.00\ \text{mol}$$

$$m=\frac{n}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}=\frac{1.00}{0.200}=5.0\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$$

**The correct molality is 5 m**, which is not among the printed options.

*Note on the printed key:* the key marks (C) 0.005 M, but 1 mol in 0.2 kg gives 5 m — neither 0.005 nor any other printed value. The options appear to have been transcribed from a different question (that set of numbers matches a *mole-fraction*-type problem). The worked answer above is the correct one for the stem as printed.

questions.question: Which of the following is a colligative property?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Decrease in freezing point

Colligative properties depend only on the **number of solute particles**, not their nature: relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, **depression of freezing point** and osmotic pressure. Freezing point falls when a solute is added because the solute lowers the chemical potential of the liquid, so solid separates at a lower temperature:

$$\Delta T_f=iK_fm$$

Option (A) is a misprint for 'relative lowering of **vapour** pressure', which is also colligative; option (B) is the wrong direction — the boiling point is *elevated*, not decreased.

questions.question: Emf of a cell with Nickel and Copper electrode will be (Given $E^\circ_{\ce{Ni^{2+}/Ni}}=-0.25$ V, $E^\circ_{\ce{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}=+0.34$ V)
questions.answer:
**(B)** +0.59 V

Copper has the more positive reduction potential, so it is the **cathode** and nickel is the anode:

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}-E^\circ_{\text{anode}}=0.34-(-0.25)=+0.59\ \text{V}$$

The cell is

$$\ce{Ni | Ni^{2+} || Cu^{2+} | Cu},\qquad \ce{Ni + Cu^{2+} -> Ni^{2+} + Cu}$$

and the positive emf means the reaction is spontaneous as written.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding a primary cell?
options: The electrode reactions can be reversed
An example of a primary cell is a mercury cell
An example of a primary cell is nickel-cadmium storage cell
questions.answer:
**(C)** An example of a primary cell is a mercury cell

A **primary cell** converts chemical energy into electricity **irreversibly** — the electrode reactions cannot be reversed by passing current in the opposite direction, so it **cannot be recharged** and must be discarded when exhausted. The **mercury cell** ($\ce{Zn-HgO}$) and the Leclanché/dry cell are primary cells. Options (A) and (B) are the defining properties of a **secondary** (storage) cell, and the nickel–cadmium cell is also secondary.

*Note on the printed key:* the tick on the paper marks (B) 'It can be recharged', which is exactly what a primary cell cannot do — the key is wrong, and (C) is correct.

questions.question: The unit of rate constant for the zero order reaction is
questions.answer:
**(C)** mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$

For a zero-order reaction $\text{rate}=k[A]^0=k$, so the rate constant *is* the rate and has the units of rate:

$$k=\frac{\text{mol L}^{-1}}{\text{s}}=\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$$

(First order gives s$^{-1}$; second order mol$^{-1}$ L s$^{-1}$.)

questions.question: A reaction in which reactant (R) are converted into products (P) follows second order kinetics. If concentration of reactant (R) is increased by 4 times, what will be the increase in rate of formation of P?
questions.answer:
**(C)** 16 times

For second-order kinetics,

$$\text{rate}=k[\ce{R}]^2$$

With $[\ce{R}]'=4[\ce{R}]$:

$$\text{rate}'=k(4[\ce{R}])^2=16k[\ce{R}]^2=16\,\text{rate}$$

So the rate of formation of P — and hence the rate of the reaction — becomes **16 times** larger. In general an $n^{th}$-order reaction multiplies the rate by $4^n$ for a fourfold increase in concentration.

questions.question: What is the order of reaction of the graph of concentration versus time shown below? (concentration decreases linearly with time, slope = −k)
questions.answer:
**(A)** Zero order

For a zero-order reaction the integrated rate law is

$$[\ce{A}]=[\ce{A}]_0-kt$$

which is a **straight line with slope $-k$** when concentration is plotted against time. A first-order reaction would give an exponential decay, and a straight line only on a plot of $\log[\ce{A}]$ versus $t$. Since the graph falls linearly, the order is zero — the rate is independent of concentration.

questions.question: Value of $t_{1/2}$ for first order reaction is given as
questions.answer:
**(B)** $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{0.693}{k}$

For a first-order reaction, $\ln\dfrac{[\ce{R_0}]}{[\ce{R}]}=kt$. At the half-life $[\ce{R}]=\frac{[\ce{R_0}]}{2}$, so

$$kt_{1/2}=\ln2=2.303\log2=2.303\times0.3010=0.693$$

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$$

The half-life is thus independent of the initial concentration — the defining test of first-order kinetics.

questions.question: The elements with Anomalous electronic configuration in the 3d series are of
questions.answer:
**(D)** Cr and Cu

A completely filled or exactly half-filled subshell has extra stability, so an electron is promoted from 4s to 3d:

$$\ce{Cr (Z=24)},\ [\ce{Ar}]\,3d^54s^1\quad(\text{not } 3d^44s^2)$$

$$\ce{Cu (Z=29)},\ [\ce{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^1\quad(\text{not } 3d^94s^2)$$

Chromium gains the stable half-filled $3d^5$ and copper the stable fully filled $3d^{10}$. No other 3d element shows this anomaly.

questions.question: Lanthanoid contraction is due to increase in
questions.answer:
**(B)** effective nuclear charge

Across the lanthanoid series the new electrons enter the **deeply buried $4f$ subshell**, which shields the outer electrons poorly. So as the nuclear charge rises the **effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons increases**, and the atoms and ions contract steadily — the **lanthanoid contraction** (about 15 pm in total from La to Lu). Its consequences are the near-identical chemistry of the lanthanoids and the slightly smaller size of the 5d elements (e.g. Zr ≈ Hf).

questions.question: Which of the following complexes is homoleptic?
questions.answer:
**(A)** [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]$^{3+}$

A **homoleptic** complex contains only **one kind of ligand**; a heteroleptic complex contains more than one. $[\ce{Co(NH3)6}]^{3+}$ has six ammine ligands only, so it is homoleptic. The others all mix ammine/aqua with chloride, so they are heteroleptic.

questions.question: An example of bidentate ligand is
questions.answer:
**(B)** C$_2$O$_4^{2-}$

The **oxalate ion**, $\ce{C2O4^{2-}}$, has two carboxylate oxygens that can both donate a lone pair, so it binds through **two donor atoms** and forms a five-membered chelate ring — it is **bidentate**. Cyanide and nitrite are monodentate (nitrite is ambidentate but still donates through one atom), and carbonate normally acts as a monodentate ligand.

questions.question: Tertiary alkyl halide among the following is
questions.answer:
**(D)** 3-chloro-3-methyl pentane

A tertiary halide has the halogen on a carbon attached to **three other carbons**. In 3-chloro-3-methylpentane,

$$\ce{CH3CH2-C(Cl)(CH3)-CH2CH3}$$

the C-3 carbon carries a chloro, a methyl and two ethyl groups — three carbon neighbours — so it is **tertiary**. 2-Chlorobutane and secondary butyl chloride are the same secondary compound, and isobutyl chloride, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2Cl}$, is primary.

questions.question: Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their boiling points: (i) (CH$_3$)$_2$CH—CH$_2$—Br (ii) CH$_3$—CH$_2$—CH$_2$—CH$_2$Br (iii) (CH$_3$)$_3$C—Br
questions.answer:
**(C)** (iii) < (i) < (ii)

Boiling point depends on **molecular surface area**: the more branched the chain, the more nearly spherical the molecule, the smaller the van der Waals contact area, and the lower the boiling point.

- (iii) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, $\ce{(CH3)3CBr}$ — highly branched, most compact: **b.p. ≈ 73 °C**
- (i) 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2Br}$ — one branch: **b.p. ≈ 91 °C**
- (ii) 1-bromobutane, straight chain — largest surface area: **b.p. ≈ 102 °C**

So the increasing order is **(iii) < (i) < (ii)**.

*Note on the printed key:* the tick marks (B) (i) < (ii) < (iii), which would make the most branched isomer boil highest — the opposite of the established order (tert-butyl bromide boils some 29 °C below 1-bromobutane). (C) is correct.

questions.question: C$_6$H$_5$OH + 3HNO$_3$(conc.) → 'A' + 3H$_2$O. Product 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(D)** 2,4,6-trinitrophenol

The —OH group is strongly activating and **ortho/para directing**, so with concentrated nitric acid all three available positions are nitrated:

$$\ce{C6H5OH + 3HNO3(conc.) -> 2,4,6-(NO2)3C6H2OH + 3H2O}$$

The product, **2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid)**, is a yellow solid and a strong acid for a phenol because the three nitro groups withdraw electron density from the ring and stabilise the phenoxide ion.

questions.question: Mark the correct order of decreasing acid strength of the following compounds: (a) phenol (b) o-nitrophenol (c) o-methoxyphenol
questions.answer:
**(A)** b > a > c

The —NO$_2$ group is strongly **electron-withdrawing** ($-I$, $-M$) and, being ortho, stabilises the phenoxide ion by resonance and by inductive withdrawal of electron density from the O–H bond — so o-nitrophenol is **more acidic** than phenol ($\text{p}K_a$ ≈ 7.2 vs 10).

The —OCH$_3$ group is **electron-releasing** by resonance ($+M$), which intensifies the negative charge on the phenoxide oxygen and destabilises the ion, so o-methoxyphenol (guaiacol) is **less acidic** than phenol.

Hence the decreasing order of acid strength is **(b) > (a) > (c)**.

questions.question: In Clemmensen reduction, carbonyl compound is reacted with
questions.answer:
**(A)** Zinc amalgam + HCl

The **Clemmensen reduction** uses **zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid** to reduce an aldehyde or ketone all the way to the hydrocarbon:

$$\ce{R-CO-R' ->[Zn/Hg][conc. HCl] R-CH2-R'}$$

The strongly acidic medium is why it is chosen for compounds that would not survive the basic Wolff–Kishner conditions. Sodium amalgam is a different (milder) reductant used for esters and for desulphonylation.

questions.question: The oxidation of toluene to benzaldehyde by chromyl chloride is called
questions.answer:
**(A)** Etard reaction

Toluene is treated with **chromyl chloride, $\ce{CrO2Cl2}$**, in carbon disulphide or dichloromethane, giving a chromium complex that is hydrolysed to **benzaldehyde**:

$$\ce{C6H5CH3 ->[CrO2Cl2][CS2] C6H5CH(Cl)O-Cr... ->[H3O^+] C6H5CHO}$$

It stops at the aldehyde because the methyl group is oxidised only once; further oxidation to benzoic acid does not occur. (Reimer-Tiemann gives salicylaldehyde from phenol; Stephen reduces a nitrile to an aldehyde; Cannizzaro disproportionates an aldehyde with no $\alpha$-H.)

questions.question: Which of the following does not give aldol condensation reaction?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Benzaldehyde

Aldol condensation needs at least one **$\alpha$-hydrogen** so that a carbanion can be generated by the base. **Benzaldehyde**, $\ce{C6H5CHO}$, has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon's neighbour (the ring carbon carries none), so it cannot form an enolate and undergoes **Cannizzaro** disproportionation with concentrated alkali instead. Acetaldehyde and acetone have acidic $\alpha$-hydrogens, and cyclohexanecarbaldehyde has an $\alpha$-H on the ring carbon, so all three give aldol products.

questions.question: One of the reagents for Sandmeyer reaction is
questions.answer:
**(B)** CuBr/HBr

In the **Sandmeyer reaction** a benzene diazonium salt is treated with a **copper(I) halide in the corresponding halogen acid**, and the diazonium group is replaced by halogen:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + CuCl/HCl -> C6H5Cl + N2 ^ + CuCl2}$$

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Br^- + CuBr/HBr -> C6H5Br + N2 ^ + CuBr2}$$

The Cu(I) salt is the reagent; copper metal with HBr (the **Gattermann** variant) also works, so (A) is the Gattermann reagent rather than the Sandmeyer one.

questions.question: Hinsberg's reagent which is used to test amines is
questions.answer:
**(C)** Benzene sulphonyl chloride

**Hinsberg's reagent** is **benzenesulphonyl chloride, $\ce{C6H5SO2Cl}$**. It reacts with primary and secondary amines but not tertiary ones, and the products differ in alkali solubility, so it distinguishes the three classes:

- **1° amine** → $\ce{C6H5SO2NHR}$ with one H on N; acidic, **soluble in KOH**.
- **2° amine** → $\ce{C6H5SO2NR2}$ with no H on N; **insoluble** in alkali.
- **3° amine** → no reaction (no H on N).

This is why the test separates primary, secondary and tertiary amines.

questions.question: Glucose and fructose are
questions.answer:
**(A)** Isomers of each other

Both have the molecular formula $\ce{C6H12O6}$, so they are **isomers** — specifically **functional isomers**, since glucose is an **aldohexose** (an aldehyde group, $\ce{-CHO}$) and fructose a **ketohexose** (a ketone group, $\ce{-CO-}$ at C-2). They are not homologues (same formula, not differing by $\ce{CH2}$), not anomers (anomers differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon of the same sugar), and not enantiomers (they are not mirror images).

questions.question: Curdling of milk is an example of
options: breaking of protein into amino acids
questions.answer:
**(D)** denaturation of proteins

Curdling (coagulation) of milk happens when the pH falls or rennet is added: the globular milk protein **casein** loses its native folded structure — its hydrogen bonds and salt bridges are disrupted — and the unfolded chains aggregate and precipitate. This is **denaturation**, a change of secondary and tertiary structure without breaking peptide bonds. The protein is not hydrolysed to amino acids and lactose is untouched.

questions.question: Which base is not found in DNA?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Uracil (U)

DNA contains the purines **adenine and guanine** and the pyrimidines **cytosine and thymine**. In RNA **uracil replaces thymine**, so uracil is not a constituent of DNA — the other difference being the sugar (2-deoxy-D-ribose in DNA, D-ribose in RNA).

questions.question: What is the sign of ΔG for electrolytic cell?
questions.answer:
For an **electrolytic cell, ΔG is positive**.

Electrolysis is a **non-spontaneous** process — electrical energy must be supplied to drive the reaction, which is the reverse of the spontaneous cell reaction. Since

$$\Delta G=-nFE_{\text{cell}}$$

and the cell emf $E_{\text{cell}}$ for the reaction as written is **negative**, $\Delta G>0$. Work must be done on the system, which is exactly what the external battery supplies. (For a galvanic cell the reverse holds: $E_{\text{cell}}>0$ and $\Delta G<0$.)

questions.question: Calculate the order of a reaction which has the following rate expression: Rate = k[A]$^2$[B].
questions.answer:
The order is the sum of the powers of the concentration terms:

$$\text{order}=2+1=3$$

The reaction is **third order overall** — second order with respect to A and first order with respect to B. The rate constant then has the units mol$^{-2}$ L$^2$ s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Which element of the 3d series of the transition metals exhibits the largest number of oxidation states?
questions.answer:
**Manganese (Mn, Z = 25).**

With the configuration $[\ce{Ar}]\,3d^54s^2$, manganese can use any number of its seven valence electrons, so it shows oxidation states from **+2 to +7** — +2, +3, +4, +5, +6 and +7 — more than any other 3d element. The +2 state ($3d^5$, half-filled) and the +7 state (permanganate, $\ce{MnO4^-}$) are the most important. (Neighbouring Cr shows +2 to +6 and Fe +2, +3 and +6, but not the full range.)

questions.question: What type of isomerism is shown by the complex [Cr(H$_2$O)$_5$(NCS)]$^{2+}$?
questions.answer:
**Linkage (ligand) isomerism.**

The thiocyanate ion, $\ce{SCN^-}$, is an **ambidentate ligand** — it can attach to the metal through either the **sulphur** or the **nitrogen** atom. The two isomers are therefore

$$\ce{[Cr(H2O)5(SCN)]^{2+}}\ (\text{S-bonded, thiocyanato})\quad\text{and}\quad \ce{[Cr(H2O)5(NCS)]^{2+}}\ (\text{N-bonded, isothiocyanato})$$

They differ in colour, in the position of the charge-transfer band, and in their reactivity — linkage isomerism arises only with ambidentate ligands such as $\ce{SCN^-}$, $\ce{NO2^-}$ and $\ce{CN^-}$.

questions.question: Why has propanol higher boiling point than propane?
questions.answer:
Because **propan-1-ol can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds while propane cannot**.

In propanol the O–H group has a hydrogen attached to a small, highly electronegative oxygen, so each molecule hydrogen-bonds to the oxygen of a neighbour. Breaking these bonds on vaporisation requires extra energy, and the molecules associate in the liquid. Propane, $\ce{C3H8}$, has only C–H bonds and no O–H, so its molecules are held only by weak London dispersion forces.

Hence propanol boils at about **370 K** against **231 K** for propane.

questions.question: What is Tollens' reagent?
questions.answer:
**Tollens' reagent** is an **ammoniacal silver nitrate solution** — silver nitrate solution treated with just enough dilute ammonia for the initial brown precipitate of silver oxide to dissolve, leaving the complex ion $[\ce{Ag(NH3)2}]^+$:

$$\ce{AgNO3 + NH4OH -> AgOH v ->[\text{excess }NH4OH] [Ag(NH3)2]^+ + OH^-}$$

It is a mild oxidising agent and the standard **test for an aldehyde**: the aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate and the silver is deposited as a bright **silver mirror**:

$$\ce{RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]^+ + 3OH^- -> RCOO^- + 2Ag v + 4NH3 + 2H2O}$$

Ketones do not respond, which is how the two are distinguished.

questions.question: What happens when glucose is treated with Br water?
questions.answer:
Bromine water is a **mild oxidising agent** and oxidises only the **aldehyde group** of glucose to a carboxyl group, leaving the secondary hydroxyls untouched. The product is **gluconic acid**:

$$\ce{CH2OH-(CHOH)4-CHO + Br2 + H2O -> CH2OH-(CHOH)4-COOH + 2HBr}$$

The cyclic hemiacetal ring opens for the reaction and re-closes as the gluconolactone, which hydrolyses to the acid. Because bromine water does not oxidise ketones, this is the standard test that shows glucose is an **aldose** (fructose gives no reaction).

questions.question: Draw the structure of 3-hydroxybutanal.
questions.answer:
3-Hydroxybutanal has a four-carbon chain, an **aldehyde** at C-1 and a **hydroxyl** at C-3:

$$\ce{CH3-CH(OH)-CH2-CHO}$$

Structure: $\ce{CH3}$ — $\ce{CH(OH)}$ — $\ce{CH2}$ — $\ce{CHO}$, numbered from the aldehyde end so the OH is on carbon 3. It is the aldol (β-hydroxy aldehyde) obtained when acetaldehyde undergoes aldol condensation, and on heating it loses water to give crotonaldehyde, $\ce{CH3CH=CHCHO}$.

questions.question: Name the milk sugar present in milk.
questions.answer:
**Lactose** — a disaccharide of $\beta$-D-galactose and D-glucose joined by a $\beta$-1,4-glycosidic bond, present at about 5% in milk:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[\text{lactase}] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$$

(hydrolysis giving galactose and glucose). It is a reducing sugar (it has a free anomeric OH on the glucose unit) and its digestion requires the enzyme **lactase**, whose absence causes lactose intolerance.

questions.question: Define the following: (i) Molality (ii) Mole-fraction.
questions.answer:
**(i) Molality ($m$)** is the number of **moles of solute per kilogram of solvent**:

$$m=\frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{mass of solvent in kg}}$$

Its unit is mol kg$^{-1}$. Because it is defined on masses, molality does **not change with temperature** (unlike molarity), which makes it the preferred concentration scale for colligative-property measurements.

**(ii) Mole fraction ($x$)** of a component in a mixture is the ratio of the **number of moles of that component to the total number of moles of all components**:

$$x_A=\frac{n_A}{n_A+n_B},\qquad x_A+x_B=1$$

It is dimensionless. For a solution of a non-volatile solute the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute, $\dfrac{p^\circ-p_s}{p^\circ}=x_2$.

questions.question: A solution of CuSO$_4$ is electrolysed for 10 minutes with a current of 1·5 amperes. What is the mass of copper deposited at cathode? (Atomic mass of Cu = 63 U)
questions.answer:
Cathode reaction:

$$\ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- -> Cu}$$

so 2 faraday (2 × 96500 C) deposit 63 g of copper, i.e. the equivalent mass is $63/2=31.5$ g eq$^{-1}$.

Charge passed:

$$Q=It=1.5\times(10\times60)=1.5\times600=900\ \text{C}$$

Mass deposited:

$$w=\frac{EQ}{96500}=\frac{31.5\times900}{96500}=\frac{28350}{96500}=0.294\ \text{g}$$

**About 0.294 g of copper** is deposited at the cathode. (Equivalently, $900/96500=9.33\times10^{-3}$ faraday, and half that many moles of Cu, $4.66\times10^{-3}$ mol × 63 = 0.294 g.)

questions.question: Predict which of the following ions will be coloured in aqueous solution: Cu$^+$, Sc$^{3+}$, Mn$^{2+}$.
questions.answer:
**Only Mn$^{2+}$ will be coloured.**

Colour in a transition-metal ion requires an **incompletely filled d subshell**, so that a $d$–$d$ transition can absorb visible light.

- **Cu$^+$ is $3d^{10}$** — completely filled, no unpaired electron, no $d$–$d$ transition → **colourless** (and in water it disproportionates to Cu$^{2+}$ and Cu anyway).
- **Sc$^{3+}$ is $3d^0$** — no d electrons at all → **colourless**.
- **Mn$^{2+}$ is $3d^5$** — five unpaired electrons, and although the spin-forbidden $d$–$d$ transitions are weak, the ion is **pale pink** in aqueous solution (very dilute solutions look almost colourless, which is why it is often described as faintly coloured).

So Mn$^{2+}$ is the coloured species; Sc$^{3+}$ and Cu$^+$ are colourless.

questions.question: Write the IUPAC names of the following: (a) [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$ (b) K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] (c) [CrCl$_2$(H$_2$O)$_4$]$^+$
questions.answer:
**(a) [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$** — six ammine ligands on Co(III), balanced by three chlorides:

**hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride**

**(b) K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$]** — Fe with six cyanides and an overall 4− charge, so Fe is +2 ($x+6(-1)=-4\Rightarrow x=+2$); the anionic complex takes the -ate form of the metal:

**potassium hexacyanoferrate(II)** (common name: potassium ferrocyanide)

**(c) [CrCl$_2$(H$_2$O)$_4$]$^+$** — charge +1 with two Cl$^-$ and four neutral water, so Cr is +3; ligands alphabetical, aqua before chlorido:

**tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) ion**

questions.question: Predict the products: (a) phenol + NH$_2$OH (b) benzenediazonium chloride + H$_3$PO$_2$ + H$_2$O (c) CH$_3$COC$_2$H$_5$ + Zn-Hg/HCl
questions.answer:
**(a) Phenol with hydroxylamine:** phenol does not have a carbonyl group, so the normal oxime-forming reaction cannot occur; under vigorous conditions the ring undergoes electrophilic substitution/amination, but the standard answer is that **no oxime is formed** — hydroxylamine condenses only with the C=O of aldehydes and ketones. With phenol the mixture gives mainly unchanged phenol (and, in strong alkali, some rearrangement products).

**(b) Benzenediazonium chloride with hypophosphorous acid:** this is the standard **deamination** — the diazonium group is replaced by hydrogen, giving **benzene**:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + H3PO2 + H2O -> C6H6 + N2 ^ + H3PO3 + HCl}$$

**(c) Butan-2-one with zinc amalgam and HCl (Clemmensen reduction):**

$$\ce{CH3COC2H5 ->[Zn-Hg][conc. HCl] CH3CH2CH2CH3}$$

The carbonyl group is reduced completely to a $\ce{CH2}$, giving **butane**.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following conversions? (a) Benzene to nitrobenzene (b) Benzoic acid to m-bromobenzoic acid (c) 1-chlorobutane to n-octane
questions.answer:
**(a) Benzene → nitrobenzene:** nitration with concentrated HNO$_3$ and concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ at 323–333 K:

$$\ce{C6H6 + HNO3 ->[H2SO4][323-333 K] C6H5NO2 + H2O}$$

**(b) Benzoic acid → m-bromobenzoic acid:** the —COOH group is **meta-directing**, so bromination puts Br at the meta position. Bromination of the free acid is sluggish, so the acid is first converted to a directing derivative or brominated in the presence of a strong acid/FeBr$_3$; the practical route is bromination of methyl benzoate followed by hydrolysis:

$$\ce{C6H5COOH ->[Br2][FeBr3] m-BrC6H4COOH}$$

$$(\text{via } \ce{C6H5COOCH3 ->[Br2/FeBr3] m-BrC6H4COOCH3 ->[H3O^+] m-BrC6H4COOH})$$

**(c) 1-Chlorobutane → n-octane:** the **Wurtz reaction** — coupling two molecules of the halide with sodium in dry ether:

$$\ce{2CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl + 2Na ->[\text{dry ether}] CH3(CH2)6CH3 + 2NaCl}$$

The carbon chain doubles, giving the symmetrical eight-carbon alkane.

questions.question: Differentiate between globular and fibrous proteins.
questions.answer:
| Globular proteins | Fibrous proteins |
|---|---|
| The polypeptide chain is coiled into a **compact, roughly spherical** shape | Chains run **side by side in long threads or sheets** |
| Held by hydrogen bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions within one chain | Held by intermolecular hydrogen bonds and **disulphide bridges between chains** |
| **Soluble in water** | **Insoluble in water** |
| Functional molecules — enzymes, hormones, transport and storage proteins | Structural and contractile role in the organism |
| Examples: **insulin, albumins, haemoglobin, myoglobin** | Examples: **collagen, keratin, myosin, fibrin** |

In short, globular proteins are soluble, shaped and mobile; fibrous proteins are insoluble, elongated and structural.

questions.question: Distinguish between DNA and RNA.
questions.answer:
| DNA | RNA |
|---|---|
| Sugar is **2-deoxy-D-ribose** | Sugar is **D-ribose** (an extra OH at C-2) |
| Bases: **A, G, C, thymine** — no uracil | Bases: **A, G, C, uracil** — no thymine |
| **Double helix** of two antiparallel chains held by base pairing | Usually a **single** polynucleotide strand (which may fold) |
| Very large, stable molecule in the **nucleus** (also mitochondria/chloroplasts) | Smaller, shorter-lived; found in the nucleus **and cytoplasm** |
| **Self-replicating**; stores and transmits genetic information | Not self-replicating; carries out protein synthesis as mRNA, tRNA and rRNA |

Both are polymers of nucleotides (base + sugar + phosphate) joined by 3′,5′-phosphodiester bonds.

questions.question: Calculate the mass of ascorbic acid (Vitamin C, C$_6$H$_8$O$_6$) to be dissolved in 75 g of acetic acid to lower its melting point by 1·5°C. $K_f=3·9$ K kg mol$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
The depression of freezing point is

$$\Delta T_f=K_f\,m$$

so the molality needed is

$$m=\frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f}=\frac{1.5}{3.9}=0.3846\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$$

For 75 g (0.075 kg) of acetic acid the moles of ascorbic acid required are

$$n=m\times\text{kg of solvent}=0.3846\times0.075=0.02885\ \text{mol}$$

Molar mass of $\ce{C6H8O6}$:

$$M=6(12)+8(1)+6(16)=72+8+96=176\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

$$w=nM=0.02885\times176=5.08\ \text{g}$$

**About 5.1 g of ascorbic acid** must be dissolved in 75 g of acetic acid to depress the freezing point by 1.5 K. (Ascorbic acid is a non-electrolyte, so $i=1$.)

questions.question: In a reaction between A and B, the initial rate of a reaction ($r_0$) was measured for different initial concentrations of A and B as given below: (A) 0·20 0·20 0·40 mol L$^{-1}$; (B) 0·30 0·10 0·05 mol L$^{-1}$; $r_0$: 5·07×10$^{-5}$, 5·07×10$^{-5}$, 1·43×10$^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$. What is the order of the reaction with respect to A and B?
questions.answer:
**Order with respect to B.** Compare runs 1 and 2, where [A] is unchanged at 0.20 M but [B] falls from 0.30 to 0.10 M:

$$\frac{r_2}{r_1}=\left(\frac{[\ce{B}]_2}{[\ce{B}]_1}\right)^y\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{5.07\times10^{-5}}{5.07\times10^{-5}}=\left(\frac{0.10}{0.30}\right)^y$$

$$1=(0.333)^y\ \Rightarrow\ y=0$$

The rate is **independent of [B]** — the reaction is **zero order in B**. This is confirmed by run 3, where [B] drops to 0.05 M with no effect on the rate beyond that of A.

**Order with respect to A.** Compare runs 1 and 3, where [A] doubles from 0.20 to 0.40 M:

$$\frac{r_3}{r_1}=\frac{1.43\times10^{-4}}{5.07\times10^{-5}}=2.82=\left(\frac{0.40}{0.20}\right)^x=2^x$$

$$x=\frac{\log 2.82}{\log2}=1.5$$

So **$x=3/2$**: the reaction is **1.5 order in A**.

**Conclusion:**

$$\text{rate}=k[\ce{A}]^{3/2}[\ce{B}]^0=k[\ce{A}]^{3/2}$$

Order in A = **1.5**, order in B = **0**, overall order = **1.5**.

*A note on the data:* the third run is the one that pins the order in A down — a rate ratio of 2.82 for a doubling of [A] can only mean $x=1.5$ (an integral first order would have given exactly 2). The reaction therefore has a fractional order, which is common in reactions with a chain or equilibrium pre-step and is exactly why order must be found by experiment.

questions.question: Draw the figure for splitting of d orbital in an octahedral crystal field.
questions.answer:
$\ce{(diagramSvg is empty; see description)}$ — In an **octahedral field** the five degenerate d orbitals split into two sets:

**Lower set — $t_{2g}$ (three orbitals, energy lowered by $0.4\Delta_o$):** $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$, $d_{xz}$. These lie **between** the axes, so their lobes point away from the six ligands and they experience less repulsion.

**Upper set — $e_g$ (two orbitals, energy raised by $0.6\Delta_o$):** $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{z^2}$. These point **directly at the ligands**, so electrons in them are repelled more.

**Splitting diagram:**

$$\ce{5 degenerate d orbitals} \longrightarrow \begin{cases} e_g\ (d_{x^2-y^2},\ d_{z^2}): & +0.6\Delta_o\\[4pt] t_{2g}\ (d_{xy},\ d_{yz},\ d_{xz}): & -0.4\Delta_o\end{cases}$$

The separation is $\Delta_o=10Dq$ and is called the crystal-field splitting energy. Its size depends on the ligand ($\ce{I^-<Br^-<Cl^-<F^-<H2O<NH3<CN^-<CO}$, the spectrochemical series) and on the metal's charge. If $\Delta_o$ is small the electrons occupy the upper orbitals before pairing (**high spin**, weak field); if large they pair in the lower set (**low spin**, strong field). The energy balance $3(-0.4\Delta_o)+2(+0.6\Delta_o)=0$ keeps the centre of gravity of the d levels unchanged.

questions.question: Draw the structures of the following compounds: (a) 3-bromo-4-phenyl pentanoic acid (b) 4-methyl pent-3-en-2-one (c) Salicylic acid (d) N,N-dimethyl methanamine (e) 1-chloro-4-ethyl cyclohexane
questions.answer:
**(a) 3-Bromo-4-phenylpentanoic acid** — a five-carbon acid chain, $\ce{HOOC-CH2-CH(Br)-CH(C6H5)-CH3}$: carboxyl at C-1, bromo at C-3, phenyl at C-4.

$$\ce{HOOC-CH2-CH(Br)-CH(C6H5)-CH3}$$

**(b) 4-Methylpent-3-en-2-one** — $\ce{CH3-CO-CH=C(CH3)-CH3}$: a ketone at C-2, a double bond between C-3 and C-4, and a methyl on C-4. It is mesityl oxide, the dehydration product of diacetone alcohol.

$$\ce{CH3COCH=C(CH3)2}$$

**(c) Salicylic acid** — 2-hydroxybenzoic acid: a benzene ring with $\ce{-COOH}$ at C-1 and $\ce{-OH}$ at C-2 (ortho).

$$\ce{o-HOC6H4COOH}$$

**(d) N,N-Dimethylmethanamine** — trimethylamine, $\ce{(CH3)3N}$: a nitrogen carrying three methyl groups and one lone pair; a tertiary amine, with a pyramidal shape.

$$\ce{(CH3)3N}$$

**(e) 1-Chloro-4-ethylcyclohexane** — a cyclohexane ring with Cl on C-1 and an ethyl group on C-4, i.e. the two substituents are *para* to each other on the ring: $\ce{Cl-C6H10-C2H5}$ (1,4-disubstituted).

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Sandmeyer reaction (b) Cannizzaro reaction (c) Carbylamine reaction.
questions.answer:
**(a) Sandmeyer reaction.** A benzene diazonium salt is treated with a **copper(I) halide in the corresponding halogen acid**, and the diazonium group is replaced by the halogen:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + CuCl/HCl -> C6H5Cl + N2 ^ + CuCl2}$$

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Br^- + CuBr/HBr -> C6H5Br + N2 ^ + CuBr2}$$

With CuCN/KCN it gives benzonitrile. It is the standard route from a primary aromatic amine to an aryl halide, which cannot be made directly from benzene when the required substituent is deactivating.

**(b) Cannizzaro reaction.** Aldehydes **without an $\alpha$-hydrogen** undergo **disproportionation** in the presence of concentrated alkali: one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate salt while another is reduced to the alcohol:

$$\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$$

$$\ce{2C6H5CHO + NaOH -> C6H5COONa + C6H5CH2OH}$$

So benzaldehyde gives sodium benzoate and benzyl alcohol. The key intermediate is a hydride transfer from the hydrate anion to the second aldehyde; the absence of an $\alpha$-H prevents the competing aldol route.

**(c) Carbylamine reaction.** **Primary** amines, aliphatic or aromatic, on warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give the foul-smelling **isocyanide**:

$$\ce{RNH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH ->[\Delta] RNC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> C6H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

It is the standard **test for a primary amine** — secondary and tertiary amines give no isocyanide, and the product's unbearable smell is unmistakable.

questions.question: (a) Differentiate between Order and Molecularity of a reaction. (b) A first order reaction has rate constant 200 s$^{-1}$. Calculate its half-life.
questions.answer:
**(a) Order vs molecularity.**

| Order | Molecularity |
|---|---|
| Sum of the powers of concentration terms in the **experimentally determined rate law** | Number of species that collide simultaneously in an **elementary step** |
| Found **experimentally**, from the rate data | Derived from the **mechanism** — a theoretical concept |
| May be zero, integral or **fractional** | Always a **whole number** (1, 2, 3) |
| Applies to complex reactions as well as elementary ones | Applies only to elementary reactions |
| Can be zero | Cannot be zero |

**(b) Half-life.** For a first-order reaction,

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}=\frac{0.693}{200}=3.47\times10^{-3}\ \text{s}$$

**The half-life is about 3.5 × 10$^{-3}$ s** (3.47 ms). The very large rate constant makes the reaction extremely fast — half the reactant is consumed in a few milliseconds — and $t_{1/2}$ is independent of the initial concentration.
